role: One of the Earliest Converts to Islam
Ascetic and Zahid among the Companions
summary: Abu Dharr al-Ghifari (RA) was among the earliest people to accept Islam — some accounts place him as the fourth or fifth Muslim — and he is celebrated as a model of asceticism, bluntness, and uncompromising personal piety. The Prophet ﷺ praised him as one of the most truthful individuals in the ummah.
biography:
Abu Dharr, whose full name was Jundab ibn Junadah al-Ghifari, came from the Ghifar tribe — a clan whose territory lay along the caravan routes between Makkah and Syria and which had a historical reputation as highway robbers. Abu Dharr stood apart from his tribal culture, having arrived at a form of personal monotheism before receiving news of the Prophet ﷺ's mission.

When word reached Abu Dharr that a man in Makkah was proclaiming the Oneness of Allah, he sent his brother Unays to investigate. His brother returned with mixed impressions, but Abu Dharr decided to go to Makkah himself. According to Ibn Hisham in al-Seerah al-Nabawiyyah, Abu Dharr searched for the Prophet ﷺ discreetly — Makkah was hostile territory — until Ali ibn Abi Talib (RA) guided him to the Prophet ﷺ. Abu Dharr met the Prophet ﷺ privately, heard the call to Islam, and accepted on the spot. He then went to the Masjid al-Haram and publicly declared the shahada before the Quraysh, who beat him severely. The Prophet ﷺ comforted him and sent him back to his tribe, instructing him to return when Islam became stronger.

Abu Dharr returned to his tribe and called them to Islam. Both the Ghifar and neighboring Aslam tribes accepted Islam — a significant early tribal conversion that Ibn Kathir records as one of Abu Dharr's most lasting contributions. The Prophet ﷺ praised this later, saying: 'May Allah have mercy on Abu Dharr; he walks alone, and he will die alone, and he will be resurrected alone.' (recorded by Ibn Sa'd and al-Hakim)

The Prophet ﷺ's praise of Abu Dharr was specific and consistent. In a famous hadith recorded by Muslim, the Prophet ﷺ said: 'There is no one under the sky, and no one on the earth, more truthful in speech than Abu Dharr.' (Sahih Muslim, Kitab Fada'il al-Sahaba). This testimony shaped how subsequent generations understood Abu Dharr — as a man of radical personal honesty who could not hold back truth regardless of consequence.

This bluntness extended to his deep concern about wealth and social inequality. Abu Dharr was among the most vocal Companions in warning against the accumulation of wealth and urging its distribution. He cited Quranic verses frequently — particularly from Surah al-Tawbah regarding those who hoard gold and silver — and applied them with great vigor. This brought him into tension with the expanding material prosperity of the early caliphate period. During the caliphate of Uthman ibn Affan (RA), his public statements in Syria, where he criticized what he saw as excessive wealth among the governing class, created friction with Mu'awiyah ibn Abi Sufyan, the governor of Syria. Uthman eventually asked Abu Dharr to return to Madinah, and later, at Abu Dharr's own request or upon Uthman's decision, he was asked to reside in al-Rabadha, a small settlement near Madinah.

Classical scholars, including al-Dhahabi in Siyar A'lam al-Nubala', present this episode as a case of sincere disagreement — Abu Dharr acting from deep personal conviction about zuhd (asceticism) and social justice, and Uthman governing with different priorities in a rapidly expanding and diversifying state. Al-Dhahabi notes that neither Abu Dharr's piety nor Uthman's integrity is in question. The incident does not reflect doctrinal dispute but a difference in temperament and approach.

Abu Dharr al-Ghifari died in al-Rabadha in 32 AH (652 CE), just as he had reportedly predicted — alone in the desert, with only his wife and a small group of passing travelers present. Ibn Mas'ud (RA) happened to be among those travelers and led his funeral prayer. Abu Dharr died as he had lived: simply, with no wealth and no pretension, in full conformity with the ascetic ideal he had preached throughout his life.

key_events.event: Traveled to Makkah and accepted Islam among the earliest converts — some accounts: fourth or fifth Muslim
Returned to Ghifar tribe and called them to Islam; Ghifar and Aslam tribes accepted
Joined the Prophet ﷺ in Madinah after the Hijrah
Participated in the Battle of Badr and subsequent campaigns
Public disagreements over wealth distribution in Syria; returned to Madinah and then to al-Rabadha
Died in al-Rabadha; funeral led by Abdullah ibn Mas'ud

notable_traits: Praised by the Prophet ﷺ as the most truthful in speech of the entire ummah
Radical asceticism — owned almost nothing throughout his life
Blunt and courageous in speaking truth regardless of political consequence
One of the first monotheists before Islam — a natural path to accepting the Prophet ﷺ
Converted his entire tribe through his personal example and preaching

key_relationships.brother: Unays ibn Junadah (who first investigated the Prophet ﷺ's message)
key_relationships.companion_at_death: Abdullah ibn Mas'ud (RA) led his funeral prayer
